sections.text: A smart pointer is a value that points to data stored somewhere else, and also does extra work for you. The simplest one is Box<T>. It puts a value on the heap, the big area of memory for data whose size can change or isn't known up front. The Box itself is small and sits where any other variable would. It owns the heap data, and when the Box goes out of scope, the data is freed.

For a plain number you would never bother with a Box. It becomes useful in three situations. The first is a type that contains itself. Imagine a list where each item holds a number and the rest of the list. Here is a first try. This code does not compile. Rust reports E0072: recursive type List has infinite size.

Rust must know how many bytes a List takes. A Cons holds a List, which holds a Cons, and so on forever. The fix is to store the rest of the list behind a Box. A Box always has the same size (it is just a pointer), so the size is known.

Cons and Nil are the two variants of the enum. A Cons holds a number and a Box with the rest of the list; Nil marks the end. The line use List::{Cons, Nil}; lets us write Cons instead of List::Cons. In sum, we match on a reference, so value is a &i32 and *value is the number itself. rest is a reference to a Box<List>, and Rust lets us pass it where a &List is expected. The next lesson explains why.

The second situation is mixing different types in one collection. A Vec holds one type, but sometimes you want a Vec of things that only share some behavior. Suppose Shape is a trait, and Circle and Square both implement it. The type dyn Shape means "some value of any type that implements Shape". It is called a trait object. Rust only decides which area method to call when the program runs. Circle and Square have different sizes, so Rust can't know the size of a dyn Shape while compiling. It must sit behind a pointer such as Box, which always has one size. Box<dyn Shape> is a box holding any Shape.
The third situation is moving a large value around without copying it. Moving a Box only copies the pointer, not all the data behind it. This matters less often, so it is enough to know it exists.

Memory has two main areas. The stack is fast and tidy, for values whose size is known when the program is compiled, such as numbers. The heap is for data that can grow or has an unknown size, such as the text inside a String. You've used the heap already: String and Vec keep their contents there. A Box is the plain, do-nothing-else way to put one value on the heap.

Coming from C++: Box<T> is like std::unique_ptr<T>. It has one owner and frees its data automatically. There is no garbage collector and no manual delete. Box<dyn Trait> is like a base-class pointer with virtual methods (dynamic dispatch through a vtable). With generics, in contrast, Rust generates a separate copy of the code for each type (static dispatch). Use Box<dyn Trait> when you need different types in one place at run time.

exercise.prompt: Add a function length(list: &List) -> u32 that counts the items: a Cons counts as 1 plus the length of the rest, and Nil is 0. Follow the shape of sum. Then change the println! in main so it prints both: sum = 6, length = 3

quiz.question: Why does enum List { Cons(i32, List), Nil } fail to compile?
options: An enum cannot have a variant that holds another variant
A Cons would contain a List that contains a Cons, so its size is infinite
i32 cannot be stored inside an enum variant

quiz.question: Where does a Box<T> keep the value of type T?
options: On the stack, inside the Box variable
Copied into every variable that uses the Box
On the heap, with the Box holding a pointer to it

quiz.question: What does Vec<Box<dyn Shape>> let you do?
options: Store values of different types that all implement Shape
Store values of any types, with no common trait needed
Store only Circles, because the Box fixes the type
